title: Build-A-Pet
brief: Design your own kind of thing with a class. The blueprint stores a name and a sound, and every pet you stamp out of it can talk. The __init__ is written for you.

problem.goal: Finish the speak() method so it prints the pet's name and sound, then create a Pet from the name the player types and make it speak.
rules: speak() must use the object's own attributes, not the word Buddy typed into the method.
The pet is created with the name the player typed and the sound "Woof".
Creating the object is not enough on its own: nothing prints until speak() is called.

steps: The Pet class already stores a name and a sound in __init__, which is done for you.
Finish the speak() method so it prints, for example: Buddy says Woof!
Below the class, the program asks the player to name their pet.
Make a Pet called my_pet using that name and the sound "Woof".
Call my_pet.speak(), then press Check project.
starterCode:
# 🐾 Build-A-Pet: make your own pet that can talk!

class Pet:
    # __init__ stores each pet's name and sound (done for you):
    def __init__(self, name, sound):
        self.name = name
        self.sound = sound

    # 1) Finish this method so it prints, for example:  Buddy says Woof!
    def speak(self):
        pass    # replace this line


name = input("Name your pet: ")

# 2) Make a Pet called my_pet with that name and the sound "Woof"


# 3) Make it speak
hints: Inside speak(), the pet's own values are self.name and self.sound. Using the plain word name in there would reach for the wrong thing entirely.
You can join text with plus signs: print(self.name + " says " + self.sound + "!"). Mind the spaces inside the quotes, or the words run together.
Step 2 creates the object: my_pet = Pet(name, "Woof"). The order matters, because __init__ expects the name first and the sound second.
Step 3 is a call on the object you just made: my_pet.speak(). You do not pass self yourself, because Python fills that in for you.
If nothing prints at all, check that you actually called speak(). Creating the object only runs __init__, which stores values silently.
inputHint: Type a name for your pet.
successMessage: It is alive! You wrote a class, gave it a method that uses its own attributes, and stamped a real object out of your blueprint. That is object oriented programming in miniature.
